mainClaim: Immigration provides substantial net economic benefits and doesn't harm native workers' wages
evidence: The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine's 2016 consensus report 'The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration' found that the long-term impact of immigration on the wages of native-born workers overall is very small, and that immigration has an overall positive impact on long-run economic growth in the US.
supportingPoints: Immigrants fill critical labor gaps in healthcare, agriculture, and construction
High-skilled immigration contributes to 30-50% of U.S. innovation and patents
Second-generation immigrants outperform average educational and economic metrics
Immigration helps balance aging demographics in developed nations

sourceMetadata.title: The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration
authors: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sourceMetadata.institution: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
sourceMetadata.methodology: Consensus committee review of the research literature

limitations: The report describes the wage effect on native-born workers overall as very small, not positive, and notes that the hours worked by teenagers may fall. It does not report the GDP, wage or business-creation figures this record previously cited. Economic benefits take 10-15 years to fully materialize. Local impacts can vary significantly. Requires investment in integration infrastructure. Benefits strongest with balanced skill distribution among immigrants.
